context: Hachikō had lived with Ueno only 15 months before Ueno's death. The Akita breed's loyalty + persistence is documented in the breed standards. The Hachikō statue was unveiled in 1934 with the dog himself present at the ceremony.

question: Bucephalus, Alexander the Great's warhorse, was reportedly tamed by the 12-year-old future emperor when no adult could mount the violent stallion. Plutarch's biography records Alexander's insight that:
answer: The horse was terrified of its own shadow
choices: The horse was terrified of its own shadow
The horse needed a special saddle imported from Persia
The horse responded to a specific Macedonian dialect command word
The horse needed to be approached only after sunset
context: Alexander rode Bucephalus throughout his conquests — across Persia, Egypt, into India. The horse died after the Battle of the Hydaspes (326 BCE) in present-day Pakistan. Alexander founded the city of Bucephala on the Jhelum River in his horse's honor. The Plutarch story illustrates Alexander's young observational genius — a sign of the future strategist.

question: Roman emperor Caligula (37-41 CE) reportedly so loved his horse Incitatus that he:
answer: Stabled him in a marble stall with ivory manger, fed him gold-flecked oats
choices: Stabled him in a marble stall with ivory manger, fed him gold-flecked oats
Released him to the streets as a public attraction
Sacrificed him as a religious offering to Jupiter
Sold him to a Gallic chieftain for political alliance
context: Suetonius (writing ~70 years after Caligula's reign) is the source. Modern historians debate whether the consul rumor was Caligula's actual intent, a satirical gesture (mocking the Senate by suggesting his horse could do their work), or imperial-propaganda character assassination by later writers. Caligula was assassinated in 41 CE — his reign included other extravagances + cruelties. The Incitatus story is one of the most repeated 'crazy emperor' anecdotes; the truth is uncertain.

question: The plains buffalo (American bison) was central to Plains Indigenous nations' material + spiritual life. A single bison provided:
answer: Meat (preserved as pemmican for travel), hide (tipi covers, robes
choices: Meat (preserved as pemmican for travel), hide (tipi covers, robes
Only meat, with no further utilization
Only ceremonial use, with the meat discarded
Only hides, used exclusively as clothing
context: The completeness of bison utilization was an honest 'no waste' tradition. The deliberate near-extinction of the bison (1865-1883) was directly aimed at destroying Plains nations' subsistence + cultural foundations. The buffalo's near-extinction is part of the same record as Western achievements — neither romanticized away nor used to define the entirety of American history.

question: Modern pet industry size in the United States exceeds approximately:
answer: $140 billion per year as of recent estimates
choices: $140 billion per year as of recent estimates
$10 million per year — a niche economic sector
$140 trillion per year — exceeding the world GDP
Zero; pet keeping is not commercialized in the US
context: The economic scale reflects long cultural trends — the Victorian era saw the explosion of formal pet-keeping among the middle class. Modern American pet expenditure has tripled in real terms over 25 years. The pet-care professional sector (groomers, walkers, sitters, trainers) is now substantial. Specialized veterinary care has approached human-medical complexity. The bank presents this as a real cultural phenomenon without moralizing.

question: The Kentucky Derby is the oldest continuously held US sporting event, run on the first Saturday in May since:
answer: 1875 — at Churchill Downs in Louisville, Kentucky
choices: 1875 — at Churchill Downs in Louisville, Kentucky
context: Secretariat's 1973 Triple Crown remains legendary — winning the Belmont Stakes by 31 lengths in a time still unbeaten. Secretariat's heart at autopsy weighed ~22 pounds (~3x normal Thoroughbred heart size). Thirteen horses have won the Triple Crown (1919-2018). The Triple Crown requires winning three different distance races (1.25, 1.1875, 1.5 miles) within five weeks — testing speed, stamina, and recovery. The Kentucky Derby has become a major American cultural event beyond horse racing.

question: Bullfighting in Spain — the corrida — remains a contested cultural tradition. The practice involves six stages culminating in the matador's faena + estocada (the killing thrust). Catalonia banned bullfighting in 2010, the Balearic Islands in 2017. The remaining Spanish regions:
choices: Made bullfighting mandatory for all citizens
context: Spanish bullfighting traces to pre-Roman Iberian + Roman venatio traditions. The modern corrida codified in the 18th century. Portuguese bullfighting (tourada) is structurally different — primarily cavaleiros (horseback) + the bull is not killed in the arena. Hemingway + Picasso made the Spanish corrida iconic to outside audiences.

question: Recent biological research into the gut microbiome of termites, cattle, and other cellulose-digesting animals has revealed that no animal actually digests cellulose by itself. The work is done by:
answer: Symbiotic gut microbes — bacteria, archaea, and protozoa secreting cellulase enzymes
choices: Symbiotic gut microbes — bacteria, archaea, and protozoa secreting cellulase enzymes
A specialized stomach enzyme produced by termite-cattle ancestors over millions of years
Mechanical grinding by gizzard stones that pulverize cellulose into glucose
Photosynthetic cells in the gut lining that convert plant matter directly to nutrients
context: Termite hindguts contain over 200 microbial species. Cattle rumen ecology scales the same principle up. Methane emissions from cattle are a microbial byproduct. Some termite species cannot digest at all when antibiotic-treated.

question: The Permian-Triassic boundary (~252M years ago) preserves a thick fungal-spore-rich layer (the 'fungal spike') just above the boundary in many sections worldwide, suggesting:
answer: Mass die-off of plants + animals leaving vast organic matter for fungi; recovery took ~5-10M years
choices: Mass die-off of plants + animals leaving vast organic matter for fungi; recovery took ~5-10M years
An asteroid impact identical to the K-Pg event in size + timing
A normal background period with no extinction signal at all
An ice age that briefly froze most marine ecosystems globally
context: The fungal spike interpretation has critics — some argue the markers are algal — but the disturbance signal is undisputed. The aftermath saw the rise of Triassic archosaurs and eventual dinosaur dominance.

question: Trilobites — three-lobed marine arthropods of the Paleozoic — were among the most successful animal groups ever, lasting from the Cambrian (~520M BP) to the end of the Permian (~252M BP). Their disappearance:
answer: Was part of the end-Permian mass extinction; trilobites had already declined dramatically before the final blow
choices: Was part of the end-Permian mass extinction; trilobites had already declined dramatically before the final blow
Occurred at the K-Pg boundary alongside the non-avian dinosaurs
Resulted from competition with bony fish that suddenly outcompeted them
Has never actually been documented; trilobites survive in deep ocean trenches
context: Over 20,000 trilobite species are known. They were the first known animals with complex eyes — calcite lenses in some species. Their disappearance ended a uniquely diverse arthropod radiation.

question: The ammonites — coiled-shelled cephalopods of the Mesozoic — diversified into thousands of species and serve as index fossils for stratigraphic correlation. They went extinct at:
answer: The K-Pg boundary 66M years ago; their living relatives include nautilus, octopus, squid, and cuttlefish
choices: The K-Pg boundary 66M years ago; their living relatives include nautilus, octopus, squid, and cuttlefish
The end-Permian extinction along with the trilobites
Only the late Pleistocene, hunted by early modern humans
Ammonites are not extinct; they survive in deep-ocean abyssal zones
context: Ammonite shells show beautiful suture patterns used to identify species + dates with precision. Some reached 2.5 m in diameter. The chambered nautilus is not a direct ammonite descendant.

question: Australia was isolated as a continent from ~30M years ago, allowing marsupial mammals to diversify in isolation. The major lineage of placental mammals successfully reaching Australia naturally was:
answer: Bats and rodents — which can fly or raft on debris across ocean gaps
choices: Bats and rodents — which can fly or raft on debris across ocean gaps
Antelopes and primates from Indonesia via a Miocene land bridge
Polar bears from Antarctica via a connecting ice corridor
All Australian mammals are placental; marsupials are confined to the Americas
context: Tasmanian devil, thylacine, sugar glider, wombat, kangaroo — Australian marsupials evolved striking convergent forms. Dingoes arrived ~5,000 BP with humans. Rabbits + foxes introduced by Europeans caused ecological devastation.

question: Lake Victoria cichlid fishes provide a textbook case of explosive evolutionary diversification. The Victoria cichlids:
answer: Radiated into ~500 species in roughly 15,000 years; many lost to introduced Nile perch + eutrophication since 1980s
choices: Radiated into ~500 species in roughly 15,000 years; many lost to introduced Nile perch + eutrophication since 1980s
Speciate slowly over millions of years like most fish groups
Have no documented evolution; the genus has been invariant since the Cretaceous
Originated from Atlantic Ocean migrations through Suez
context: Nile perch (Lates niloticus), introduced in the 1950s for fisheries, drove ~40% of endemic cichlid species to extinction. Lake Malawi + Lake Tanganyika cichlid radiations are even older + more diverse.

question: The peppered moth (Biston betularia) is a classic textbook example of natural selection in industrial-revolution Britain. Pre-industrial moths were light-colored; during pollution, dark forms increased dramatically. The mechanism:
answer: Bird predation — pollution killed lichens, exposing dark bark; light moths became visible and were eaten
choices: Bird predation — pollution killed lichens, exposing dark bark; light moths became visible and were eaten
Direct mutation caused by air pollution, with no selection involved
Migration of dark moths from continental Europe into Britain
Choice by moths to land on bark matching their color
context: Bernard Kettlewell's 1950s experiments supported the bird-predation mechanism. Michael Majerus (2012) repeated the work with corrected methods + confirmed the original finding. Clean Air Acts (1956 UK) reversed the trend.

question: Stephen Jay Gould and Niles Eldredge proposed 'punctuated equilibrium' in 1972 — the idea that species typically remain morphologically stable for long periods, with most evolutionary change in brief speciation events. The model:
choices: Was universally rejected by all paleontologists by 1980
Was identical to Lamarckian inheritance of acquired characteristics
context: Punctuated equilibrium does not contradict Darwinian evolution by natural selection — it concerns pattern, not mechanism. Gould's prolific writing made him one of the most public scientists of his era.

question: Endosymbiosis — the theory that mitochondria and chloroplasts originated as engulfed bacteria — was championed by Lynn Margulis from 1967 onward. The evidence:
answer: Mitochondria + chloroplasts have own DNA, ribosomes, double membranes; they divide independently like bacteria
choices: Mitochondria + chloroplasts have own DNA, ribosomes, double membranes; they divide independently like bacteria
No evidence; the theory was abandoned by 1980
Direct microscopic observation of bacteria being engulfed in modern human cells
Endosymbiosis only applies to plant chloroplasts, never animal mitochondria
context: Margulis's foundational 1967 paper was rejected by 15 journals before publication. Her insight is now textbook biology. Eukaryotic cells are themselves ecosystems of formerly free-living organisms.

question: The ediacaran fauna (~580-540 million years ago) preserves the earliest known complex multicellular animals. Forms like Dickinsonia, Spriggina, Charnia, and Kimberella were:
answer: Soft-bodied, lacking hard parts, generally sessile or slow-moving
choices: Soft-bodied, lacking hard parts, generally sessile or slow-moving
Microscopic single-celled bacteria with no body plan
Modern vertebrates fully developed before the Cambrian
context: Dickinsonia 2018 cholesterol biomarker discovery (Bobrovskiy et al., Science) established it as a definite animal. The Ediacaran 'frondose' creatures probably absorbed nutrients across their surface.

question: Pterosaurs (Late Triassic to end-Cretaceous) were not dinosaurs but a separate group of flying reptiles. The largest known, Quetzalcoatlus northropi from Texas, had a wingspan up to ~11 m. Recent biomechanical research suggests Quetzalcoatlus:
answer: Walked quadrupedally + pole-vaulted into flight off its forelimbs — not bipedal bird-style launch
choices: Walked quadrupedally + pole-vaulted into flight off its forelimbs — not bipedal bird-style launch
Was permanently airborne and never landed during its life
Was actually a swimming reptile that could not fly at all
Hunted exclusively from elevated cliff perches and never walked
context: Michael Habib's models showed bird-style launches cannot lift Quetzalcoatlus's mass (~250+ kg). They went extinct at the K-Pg boundary; only true birds survived among flying vertebrates.

question: Modern phylogenetic methods (cladistics) classify organisms by shared derived characteristics reflecting common ancestry. Strict cladistics requires that all taxa be monophyletic. This implies:
answer: Birds are dinosaurs — surviving theropods; reptiles is paraphyletic without birds
choices: Birds are dinosaurs — surviving theropods; reptiles is paraphyletic without birds
Birds are descended from amphibians, not dinosaurs
Cladistics is the same as Linnaean classification with no differences
All animals must be classified within ten taxonomic levels
context: Willi Hennig's cladistics revolutionized systematics from 1950 onward. Modern paleontology speaks of 'non-avian dinosaurs' rather than 'dinosaurs are extinct.' Fish is also paraphyletic — does not include tetrapods.

question: Bats represent the only mammalian order to achieve true powered flight, independently of birds. Their wing is structurally:
answer: Skin (patagium) stretched between elongated finger bones
choices: Skin (patagium) stretched between elongated finger bones
Feathered like a bird's wing in every detail
A solid plate of bone identical to a sea-turtle flipper
Made of chitin like an insect's wing
context: Bats (order Chiroptera) constitute ~20% of mammal species. Their oldest fossils (~52M years ago, Onychonycteris finneyi) show wings already developed before echolocation evolved.

question: After the K-Pg extinction wiped out non-avian dinosaurs, birds survived. Which avian groups largely persisted through the post-impact recovery?
answer: Ground-dwelling and aquatic birds — perching arboreal lineages largely perished with forests
choices: Ground-dwelling and aquatic birds — perching arboreal lineages largely perished with forests
Pure random chance with no biological factors involved
Only birds in zoos at the time of impact survived
Birds escaped to other planets and returned after recovery
context: Field et al. 2018 (Current Biology) showed the surviving avian lineages were largely ground-dwellers. Tinamous + ratites descend from a single surviving ground-bird lineage that diversified globally afterward.

question: Joseph Felsenstein's introduction of maximum-likelihood and Bayesian methods to phylogenetics, from the 1980s onward, transformed evolutionary biology. The methods allow:
answer: Reconstructing trees from DNA + protein data with explicit probabilistic models accounting
choices: Reconstructing trees from DNA + protein data with explicit probabilistic models accounting
Predicting weather patterns from animal behavior
Calculating the precise color of dinosaur skin
Determining the exact day of any species' first appearance
context: Tools like MrBayes, BEAST, RAxML, IQ-TREE became standard. The advent of cheap genome sequencing in the 2000s provided the data the methods needed. Many longstanding evolutionary questions are now resolvable.

question: The earliest tetrapods — Acanthostega, Ichthyostega — emerged ~365M years ago in the late Devonian. These transitional vertebrates had:
answer: Eight digits per limb (Ichthyostega had 7); digit number was variable before stabilization
choices: Eight digits per limb (Ichthyostega had 7); digit number was variable before stabilization
Exactly five digits in the modern arrangement from the start
Wheels rather than limbs at the locomotor stage
No limbs at all; modern interpretations are mistaken
context: The polydactyly of early tetrapods was one of the great surprises of late-20th-century paleontology. The pentadactyl five-digit limb plan became fixed only later. Early tetrapods likely spent most time in water with brief terrestrial forays.

question: The molecular clock — using accumulated DNA differences between species to estimate divergence times — was proposed by Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling in 1962. The technique:
answer: Works because genetic changes accumulate at roughly constant rates
choices: Works because genetic changes accumulate at roughly constant rates
Works perfectly without any external calibration needed
Has been entirely refuted and is no longer used by biologists
Only works for plants, never animals
context: Molecular clocks allow dating of divergence events lacking fossil evidence — the human-chimpanzee split ~6-7M years ago, whales from artiodactyls ~55M years ago. Disagreements between molecular + fossil dates have spurred important research.

question: Charles Darwin's 1859 The Origin of Species depended heavily on observations of animal husbandry — pigeon breeds, dog breeds, livestock varieties. Why was this so central to his argument?
answer: Artificial selection is a fast, visible analog to natural selection
choices: Artificial selection is a fast, visible analog to natural selection
Darwin was secretly a pigeon breeder and wanted to promote his hobby
Husbandry has no relevance to evolution; the connection was discredited
Darwin only wrote about plants, never animals
context: The Origin's first chapter focuses on domesticated varieties. Darwin kept pigeons + studied many breeds. The argument from artificial selection let readers see for themselves how much variation breeders could produce.

question: Coral reefs are built primarily by scleractinian corals — animals in close symbiosis with photosynthetic dinoflagellates called zooxanthellae. The relationship explains why most reef-building corals:
answer: Live only in shallow, warm, clear waters
choices: Live only in shallow, warm, clear waters
Live exclusively in deep-sea anoxic environments far from sunlight
Are photosynthetic themselves and need no symbionts
Are mammals with internal skeletons rather than external
context: Mass coral bleaching events (1998, 2010, 2016-17, 2024) have damaged reefs globally. Corals can survive brief bleaching by reacquiring zooxanthellae; prolonged bleaching kills them. Reefs host ~25% of marine species in <1% of ocean area.

question: The fossil-record principle of 'superposition' (younger rocks lie above older rocks) was articulated by Nicolaus Steno in 1669. This principle plus uniformitarianism (Hutton, Lyell) made deep time + evolution possible. Without these:
answer: Darwin's theory could not have been formulated
choices: Darwin's theory could not have been formulated
Evolution could be proven in a single day's experiment
Evolution would still be obvious without geological context
Stratigraphic principles are unrelated to biology
context: James Hutton (Edinburgh, 1726-1797) is the founder of modern geology. Lyell's Principles of Geology (1830) heavily influenced Darwin during the Beagle voyage. Mary Anning's fossils provided concrete evidence of extinct worlds.

question: The Late Devonian Mass Extinction (~372 and ~359M BP, two pulses) is the second of the Big Five. It was especially severe for:
answer: Marine reef ecosystems — placoderms + tropical groups vanished; tetrapods survived
choices: Marine reef ecosystems — placoderms + tropical groups vanished; tetrapods survived
Only terrestrial dinosaurs; no marine impact whatsoever
Only freshwater fish, with no other groups affected
Only insects, sparing all vertebrates entirely
context: Causes are debated: anoxic ocean events (perhaps from expanding land plants), volcanism, possible asteroid impacts. Dunkleosteus, a 6-meter armored placoderm apex predator of the Devonian, went extinct in this event.

question: The Federal Humane Slaughter Act of 1958 (US) required livestock be rendered insensible to pain before slaughter at federally inspected plants. The law:
answer: Originally exempted poultry; later expanded; religious slaughter exempted
choices: Originally exempted poultry; later expanded; religious slaughter exempted
Banned all forms of meat consumption in the United States
Applied to all animals including pets and zoo animals
Required exclusive use of guillotines for cattle slaughter
context: Senator Hubert Humphrey was the primary sponsor. Modern stunning methods include captive-bolt for cattle, electrical stunning for pigs/sheep, and CO2 for pigs. Poultry coverage under HSA is still legally contested.

question: Temple Grandin, the autistic livestock-handling scientist + welfare advocate, made a distinctive contribution to industry practice:
answer: Curved slaughterhouse chutes with solid sides + careful lighting that reduce animal stress
choices: Curved slaughterhouse chutes with solid sides + careful lighting that reduce animal stress
Banning all slaughterhouses worldwide by federal mandate
Reducing cattle to producing milk only without ever being slaughtered
Eliminating animal protein from human diets globally
context: Grandin's designs are used in roughly half of US slaughterhouse capacity. Her welfare audits codified into industry standards made measurable improvements. She is a major public advocate for humane slaughter as part of a defensible meat industry.

question: The 'cage-free' vs. 'free-range' vs. 'pasture-raised' egg distinctions have specific USDA + industry definitions. The practical differences:
answer: Cage-free: indoor only. Free-range: some outdoor access. Pasture-raised: substantial outdoor rotation
choices: Cage-free: indoor only. Free-range: some outdoor access. Pasture-raised: substantial outdoor rotation
All three labels are identical with no welfare or management differences
Cage-free means the hens are kept in larger cages than conventional
Pasture-raised hens are kept in cages but with bigger windows
context: California Proposition 12 requires minimum space per laying hen + bans certain confined housing. Conventional caged eggs declined from ~95% of US production to ~60% in 15 years. Consumer preferences + regulatory shifts drive change.

question: Joel Salatin's polyculture model — chickens following cattle in rotational grazing — exploits a specific ecological relationship. The chickens:
answer: Spread cattle manure + eat fly larvae + parasites
choices: Spread cattle manure + eat fly larvae + parasites
Attack the cattle directly with their beaks for territory disputes
Compete with cattle for the same grass food source
Replace the cattle entirely after the first rotation
context: The chickens' parasite-cleaning function is the key insight. Many cattle parasites have larval stages in cow manure; chickens find these tasty. Salatin's egg-mobile + broiler-pen designs make the polyculture practical.

question: Antibiotic use in livestock — both therapeutic + sub-therapeutic 'growth promotion' use — is a major concern for antimicrobial resistance. The 2015 EU ban + 2017 US FDA guidance:
answer: Eliminated sub-therapeutic + growth-promotion use of medically important antibiotics
choices: Eliminated sub-therapeutic + growth-promotion use of medically important antibiotics
Banned all veterinary medicine for animals worldwide
Required mandatory antibiotic dosing of all animals daily
Mandated abolition of all livestock production
context: Sub-therapeutic use to boost feed efficiency drove decades of livestock productivity gains and contributed to antimicrobial resistance spread. WHO + CDC list antimicrobial resistance among top global health threats.

question: Therapy animals — distinct from service animals + emotional support animals — visit hospitals + nursing homes to comfort patients. The therapy-animal field developed rapidly after:
answer: Boris Levinson's 1962 work formalizing pet-assisted therapy
choices: Boris Levinson's 1962 work formalizing pet-assisted therapy
Therapy animals are a 21st-century invention with no scientific basis
Therapy with animals is illegal in all developed countries
All therapy animals must be exotic species like kangaroos
context: Levinson, a child psychologist, noticed his dog Jingles calmed his young patients. He published The Dog as Co-Therapist (1962). Therapy Dogs International + Pet Partners certify therapy animals. Documented benefits include reduced anxiety + lower blood pressure.

question: California's Proposition 12 (passed 2018, effective 2022) is among the strongest US state-level farm-animal welfare laws. It requires:
answer: Minimum space allowances for breeding pigs, veal calves, and laying hens
choices: Minimum space allowances for breeding pigs, veal calves, and laying hens
Banned all animal agriculture in California by 2025
Required all California pets to receive daily veterinary care
Banned all importation of food from outside California
context: Prop 12 passed 63% to 37%. The Supreme Court upheld it in National Pork Producers Council v. Ross (2023). Massachusetts Question 3 (2016) is a parallel state law. Market-wide shifts toward higher welfare standards have followed.

question: The Russian fox domestication experiment, begun by Dmitri Belyaev in 1959 and continued by Lyudmila Trut, selected silver foxes only for tameness toward humans. Within ~40 generations:
answer: The foxes developed many domestication traits
choices: The foxes developed many domestication traits
Remained completely wild and unchanged from the original population
Became gradually larger and more aggressive over each generation
Lost all reproductive capability after the third generation
context: The Belyaev study established 'domestication syndrome' as a real package of traits emerging together under tameness selection. The mechanism may involve neural crest developmental changes (Wilkins, Wrangham, Fitch 2014).

question: The American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA), founded in 1863, makes veterinary medicine one of the oldest US professional medical traditions. The discipline:
answer: Predates many human-medicine specialties in formal organization
choices: Predates many human-medicine specialties in formal organization
Has only existed since 2000 as an informal hobby practice
Is identical to human medicine with no specialized training
Is restricted to large farm animals only, never companion animals
context: The École nationale vétérinaire de Lyon (1761, France) was the first veterinary school. The discipline encompasses small animal, large animal, public health, wildlife, military, zoo, and biomedical research practice.

question: Wildlife corridors — protected habitat bands linking otherwise isolated wildlife populations — are an established conservation technique. The Yellowstone-to-Yukon initiative:
answer: Aims to protect ~3,200 km north-south corridor enabling large-mammal movement from
choices: Aims to protect ~3,200 km north-south corridor enabling large-mammal movement from
Targets only insects, with no large mammal concerns
Was abandoned in the 1990s with no continuing program
context: Highway over- + underpasses (especially Banff National Park) reduce wildlife-vehicle collisions + maintain genetic connectivity. Connectivity is increasingly central to conservation planning. Y2Y is led by Karsten Heuer + many partners.

question: The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES), signed 1973, regulates international wildlife trade. The treaty:
choices: Requires every species to be hunted to extinction
Was abandoned in the 1980s as ineffective
context: The 1989 elephant-ivory listing (Appendix I) significantly reduced ivory trade. CITES is not perfect but is the major international wildlife-protection framework. Rhino horn, tiger parts, marine species, and many orchids + cycads are listed.

question: Indigenous subsistence hunting rights — Inuit whaling + sealing, Saami reindeer herding, Aboriginal Australian hunting, Native American fishing — is a contested area of modern policy. The bank's framing:
answer: Indigenous subsistence rights have a separate moral status
choices: Indigenous subsistence rights have a separate moral status
All hunting should be banned regardless of cultural context
Indigenous hunting should be entirely unregulated worldwide
Indigenous hunting is identical to commercial hunting
context: The Marine Mammal Protection Act (1972) exempts Alaska Natives + Indigenous subsistence hunting. ICRW recognizes aboriginal subsistence whaling. The US Endangered Species Act has Native American exemptions for ceremonial use.

question: The whooping crane (Grus americana) was reduced to ~15 birds in the 1940s. Recovery efforts (captive breeding, surrogate-parented young, migration training via ultralight aircraft) have brought the wild population to:
choices: Has always had a population of ~10,000 and never needed conservation
Went extinct in 1950 with no surviving descendants
Is a mythological bird that never existed
context: 'Operation Migration' used ultralight aircraft to teach young whooping cranes their migration route. The Aransas-Wood Buffalo flock is the only natural wild whooping-crane population. The species illustrates extreme bottleneck recovery.

question: The Endangered Species Act of 1973 is among the US's most consequential environmental laws. Notable recoveries enabled by ESA listing include:
answer: Bald eagle (delisted 2007), American alligator (delisted 1987), peregrine falcon (delisted 1999)
choices: Bald eagle (delisted 2007), American alligator (delisted 1987), peregrine falcon (delisted 1999)
No species has ever been recovered under ESA listing
Only fish have benefited, never birds or mammals
ESA listing has accelerated all listed species toward extinction
context: The bald eagle recovery from DDT-poisoning + persecution is iconic. The California condor recovery (still listed) from ~22 birds in 1982 involved every-individual captive breeding + release; ~500+ now fly free.

question: Modern hunting + fishing license sales remain the foundational funding for state wildlife agencies — the 'user-pays' principle of North American conservation. Since 1980, hunter numbers have:
choices: Hunter numbers have no relationship to wildlife agency funding
All wildlife funding now comes from corporate sponsorships exclusively
context: About 5% of Americans hunt, down from ~10% in 1980. Proposals like the Recovering America's Wildlife Act would supplement funding from general taxes. The conservation model depends on its hunting + fishing communities.

question: Modern trapping is regulated by Best Management Practices (BMP) — guidelines developed through veterinary + trapper collaboration to minimize injury. BMP traps:
answer: Use offset/laminated foothold jaws + quick-kill body-gripping traps + set-time limits to
choices: Use offset/laminated foothold jaws + quick-kill body-gripping traps + set-time limits to
Have never changed since 19th-century jaw traps
Are made of explosive material that detonates on contact
Are illegal in all US states by federal mandate
context: The Agreement on International Humane Trapping Standards (1997) required modernized trap designs. Animal-rights advocates argue trapping cannot meet welfare standards; pro-trapping advocates point to documented improvements. The debate is genuinely contested.

question: Coyotes (Canis latrans) have expanded their range dramatically in the past century — from the western Great Plains across the US, into Central America, and onto urban areas across North America. The expansion was enabled by:
choices: Direct human transport to all new ranges as livestock
Climate change cooling temperatures across North America
Successful captive breeding programs releasing them in cities
context: Urban coyotes are now established in Chicago, Los Angeles, New York, and most large North American cities. Stan Gehrt's Cook County Coyote Project has tracked Chicago coyotes since 2000. They eat rats, rabbits, geese, fruit, garbage.

question: Roman haruspicy — divination from animal entrails, especially the liver — was a state-religious practice inherited from Etruscan tradition. The trained haruspex:
answer: Examined a sacrificed animal's liver for marks, color, shape
choices: Examined a sacrificed animal's liver for marks, color, shape
Counted the stars in the night sky exclusively
Read the future from the calls of wild ravens
Examined the entrails of human captives
context: Etruscan haruspicy was practiced through the Roman imperial period. Cicero's De Divinatione (44 BCE) contains both reverent + skeptical treatments. Roman generals consulted haruspices before major decisions. The discipline was a serious pattern-reading science to its practitioners.

question: Ratatoskr — the squirrel running up + down the world tree Yggdrasil in Norse mythology — has a specific role:
answer: Carrying insults between the eagle at Yggdrasil's top and the dragon Niðhöggr at the roots
choices: Carrying insults between the eagle at Yggdrasil's top and the dragon Niðhöggr at the roots
Holding up Yggdrasil with his teeth at the world's center
Guarding the gates of Asgard against frost giants
Sleeping through the entire Ragnarök without waking
context: The Ratatoskr myth appears in Grímnismál (Poetic Edda) + Snorri's Prose Edda. The squirrel as gossip-carrier is a uniquely Norse touch. Niðhöggr ('Malice-Striker') is the dragon gnawing at one of Yggdrasil's roots.

question: Marengo, Napoleon Bonaparte's white Arabian stallion (named after the 1800 Battle of Marengo), carried the emperor through major battles including Austerlitz, Jena, Wagram, the 1812 Russia campaign, and Waterloo. After Waterloo:
answer: Marengo was captured by British forces and lived until 1831 in England
choices: Marengo was captured by British forces and lived until 1831 in England
Marengo died in battle at Waterloo and was buried in France
Marengo escaped to Russia and lived another 40 years in Siberia
Marengo is entirely fictional; no such horse existed
context: Marengo stood only ~14.1 hands but was famously strong + brave. His ~38-year lifespan was exceptional. Napoleon's preference for Arabian horses (lighter, more enduring than heavy European warhorses) reshaped Continental cavalry tradition.

question: Modern Belgian Malinois military working dogs achieve roles including explosive-detection, search + rescue, and personnel-protection. Cairo, a Malinois on the 2011 Operation Neptune Spear:
answer: Participated in the SEAL Team 6 raid that killed Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad
